source.title: On the Interpretability of Whisper Encodings Using Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Dan Pluth; Z. Houghton; Yu Zhou; Vijay K. Gurbani

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. No apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: Applies a sparse autoencoder and feature-steering analyses to Whisper’s audio encoder, a new modality and model setting for the feature-recovery claims. It does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE features, feature statistics, and steering outcomes relevant to sparse feature recovery and whether SAE features are complete units. It does not test feature competition for limited capacity, neuron polysemanticity, superposition geometry, or feature dimensionality. Grid-search reconstruction losses are used to select hyperparameters, so they are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Trains a TopK SAE on Whisper base's frozen final encoder layer and reports precision and recall for recovered sparse latents, plus frame-localized steering. This is a new setting (an audio transformer encoder) for V4's dictionary-recovery claim. It also explicitly reports feature splitting and absorption, which bears on V5. No toy models, neuron-level polysemanticity analysis, capacity manipulation or feature-dimensionality tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that Whisper's encoder represents a hierarchy of information from phonetic through lexical, syntactic, morphological and semantic levels, plus non-linguistic noise and position. This exceeds what transcription strictly requires. They find diverse monosemantic SAE features, so SAE interpretability carries over to an audio encoder. Steering is easier for higher-level features and for insertion than for removal, possibly because lower-level information is encoded redundantly; they call this account preliminary.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a k-Sparse Autoencoder on Whisper base’s final encoder activations and tests identified features with frame-localized steering. It does not use the original toy-network superposition setup or measure overlap geometry.
record.method_sensitivity: Steering outcomes differ by feature level and intervention direction: lower-level features are harder to steer, and positive steering is generally more successful than negative steering. Profanity steering is also reported across English, French, and Spanish.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering asymmetry: positive steering succeeds for 5 of 6 levels, while negative steering succeeds only for profanity. Lower-level (phonetic) latents are the hardest to steer; the authors suggest redundant encoding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents in a real model are not uniformly causally sufficient or necessary: removal is less effective than insertion, and less so for low-level features.

record.problems: The study focuses on Whisper base and does not report random-latent or comparable null steering controls. Many steering results are qualitative examples rather than aggregate rates, and no confidence intervals or error bars are reported. The analysis set partially overlaps SAE training data, although the paper says most analysis data and effectively all Common Voice cross-lingual data were held out. Automated latent labels were 76% accurate on a manually evaluated subset of 100. Semantic ground-truth curation is described as coarser than other annotation procedures.
record.rows_left_out: Appendix F contains additional individually listed latent examples and automated labels, but they are not reported as separate quantitative tests of the claim; the paper says they are a broader sample. Table II and Table III provide illustrative activation samples already covered by the corresponding feature-statistic rows. Grid-search reconstruction losses were omitted because they were used to choose SAE hyperparameters.

untested.parts: No toy networks, superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transition or near-orthogonal overlap measured.
No test of capacity competition or of importance-driven dedicated dimensions.
Neuron-level polysemanticity and its causes are not studied.

Text-only LLMs are not tested, and spread of features across individual neurons is not measured. Only one model (Whisper base) and one layer are examined. There is no comparison to random or untrained baselines.
Stability across SAE seeds or sizes and canonicality across dictionaries are not tested. The authors argue that hyperparameters affect only approximation fidelity but give no empirical test.
No comparison of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Detection statistics for language-identity latent 5106 (non-English: precision 77.6%, recall 91.1%)
Positive steering of profanity latent 3584 turning 'sheet' into 'shit'
Per-latent correctness of automated labels for the Appendix F sample, as a coarse measure of interpretable fraction

record.verdict_notes: Whisper is an audio transformer, not a text LLM, so V4 support is out-of-domain for 'LLMs'. No random-latent or null steering controls are reported, and steering results are qualitative examples, not rates. Precision and recall are reported for hand-picked latents with no baseline. The analysis set partially overlaps the SAE training data.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, overlapping near-orthogonal directions, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry are not tested.
The paper does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise from competition for limited capacity or whether importance determines dedicated dimensions.
The paper does not study polysemantic neurons or alternative causes of polysemanticity.
Tests SAE feature recovery in Whisper’s audio encoder, not text-only LLMs or whether LLM activations are distributed across neurons or orthogonal directions.
Reports feature splitting and examples of incomplete feature coverage, but does not test stability across training runs, SAE configurations, or other definitions of canonicality.
Does not compare one-dimensional directions with multi-dimensional features.

relation.reason: Directly evaluates whether recovered latents track identifiable properties and affect transcripts; also reports splitting and absorption relevant to dictionary completeness.

tranche.reason: Tests dictionary recovery of interpretable sparse features in a new setting, Whisper's audio encoder, with detection measurements and causal steering.

source_check.notes: Results concern illustrative latents from one SAE; steering examples lack aggregate success rates. Precision and recall use individual occurrences, and the analysis set partially overlaps SAE training data.

statements.correction: Whisper: one 16,000-latent TopK SAE, K=45; latent 29 recall 15.7%; latent 1492 recall 37.7%; low recall attributed partly to feature splitting; profanity detection combines latents 3584 and 104; splitting and absorption explicitly reported; no comparison across SAE configurations.
statements.problem: The Whisper facts are correct, but this study does not compare dictionaries across configurations and therefore does not establish configuration invariance or its absence.
